entries.name: VLF/LF fixed and maritime mobile
entries.notes: The standard-time transmitters live here: WWVB and MSF on 60 kHz, DCF77 on 77.5 kHz. Most receivers need direct sampling or an upconverter to reach it.

entries.name: 2200 m amateur
entries.notes: 1 W EIRP in most administrations: CW, WSPR and other very slow modes.

entries.name: Maritime radio beacons and DGPS
entries.notes: Differential GPS corrections, MSK at 100–200 bit/s.

entries.name: Aeronautical non-directional beacons
entries.notes: A keyed carrier repeating a two- or three-letter Morse ident.

entries.name: 630 m amateur
entries.notes: 5 W EIRP in most administrations: CW, WSPR and FT8.

entries.name: NAVTEX — 490 kHz
entries.notes: National-language navigational warnings. SITOR-B, 100 baud FSK with a 170 Hz shift.

entries.name: Maritime mobile (MF)
entries.notes: 500 kHz was the international distress and calling frequency until 1999.

entries.name: NAVTEX — 518 kHz
entries.notes: The international NAVTEX service, always in English. SITOR-B, 100 baud FSK.

entries.name: Medium-wave broadcast
entries.notes: 9 kHz raster in Regions 1 and 3. Groundwave by day, skywave after dark.

entries.name: 160 m amateur
entries.notes: Lower sideband by convention. A night band: daytime absorption kills it.

entries.name: Maritime mobile (2 MHz)
entries.notes: 2182 kHz is the MF distress and calling frequency.

entries.name: HF aeronautical mobile (route)
entries.notes: Upper sideband. Long-haul oceanic and polar air traffic control.

entries.name: HF fixed, mobile and amateur (80 m)
entries.notes: How much of this is amateur depends on the ITU region: 3.5–3.8 MHz in Region 1, 3.5–4.0 in Region 2, 3.5–3.9 in Region 3.

entries.name: Maritime mobile (4 MHz)
entries.notes: 4207.5 kHz is the 4 MHz DSC calling channel.

entries.name: 60 m amateur
entries.notes: The WRC-15 secondary allocation: 15 W EIRP, and a band the amateur service shares with fixed and mobile users who were there first.

entries.name: ISM — 6.78 MHz
entries.notes: RR 5.138: industrial, scientific and medical.

entries.name: 40 m amateur
entries.notes: Lower sideband. 7.2–7.3 MHz is amateur in Region 2 and shortwave broadcast everywhere else, which is why 40 m sounds different depending on where you are.

entries.name: Maritime mobile (8 MHz)
entries.notes: 8414.5 kHz is the 8 MHz DSC calling channel.

entries.name: 30 m amateur
entries.notes: A WARC band: CW and narrow digital only by IARU convention, no contests, and usually a 200 W ceiling.

entries.name: HF aeronautical mobile (off-route)
entries.notes: 11175 kHz is the primary US Air Force HFGCS channel.

entries.name: Radio astronomy — 13.36 MHz
entries.notes: A passive band: no emission is permitted.

entries.name: ISM — 13.56 MHz
entries.notes: RR 5.150. NFC and HF RFID.

entries.name: 20 m amateur
entries.notes: Upper sideband above 10 MHz by convention. The band that is open somewhere almost all the time.

entries.name: 17 m amateur
entries.notes: A WARC band: no contesting by IARU convention, so it stays civil.

entries.name: 15 m amateur
entries.notes: A daytime DX band that follows the solar cycle closely.

entries.name: 12 m amateur
entries.notes: A WARC band, and the quietest of the high bands.

entries.name: ISM — 27 MHz
entries.notes: RR 5.150. The Citizens' Band channel plans sit inside it, as does a great deal of radio control and industrial heating.

entries.name: 10 m amateur
entries.notes: Dead at solar minimum and worldwide at maximum. 29.6 MHz is the FM calling channel.

entries.name: VHF low-band land mobile
entries.notes: Long-range fleet, utility and forestry radio. Sporadic-E carries it across a continent for weeks at a time in early summer.

entries.name: ISM — 40.68 MHz
entries.notes: RR 5.150. Model control and low-power telemetry.

entries.name: VHF fixed, mobile and broadcast
entries.notes: The old television Band I in Region 1; 50–54 MHz is the 6 m amateur band in Regions 2 and 3, and 50–52 MHz in most of Region 1 since WRC-19.

entries.name: Marker beacons — 75 MHz
entries.notes: Airport marker beacons, keyed at 400, 1300 or 3000 Hz.

entries.name: FM broadcast
entries.notes: ±75 kHz deviation, a 19 kHz stereo pilot, and RDS on a 57 kHz subcarrier. Region 2 starts at 88.0 MHz with a 200 kHz raster.

entries.name: VOR and ILS localizer
entries.notes: Each carries a Morse ident you can read straight off the AM audio.

entries.name: Airband — civil aviation voice
entries.notes: AM, so a stronger station does not capture a weaker one. 25 kHz spacing, 8.33 kHz across much of Europe. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency and is normally silent.

entries.name: Meteorological satellite downlink
entries.notes: NOAA APT at 137.100, 137.620 and 137.9125 MHz; Meteor-M LRPT nearby. Right-hand circular polarisation, so a linear antenna loses 3 dB.

entries.name: 2 m amateur
entries.notes: 145.500 MHz is the Region 1 FM calling channel and 144.800 MHz carries APRS. Regions 2 and 3 have 2 MHz more, up to 148 MHz.

entries.name: Marine VHF
entries.notes: Channel 16 (156.800 MHz) is distress, safety and calling; channel 70 (156.525 MHz) is DSC data only and carries no voice.

entries.name: AIS — 161.975 and 162.025 MHz
entries.notes: AIS 1 and AIS 2, 9600 baud GMSK in 25 kHz channels. Both are decoded at once if the receiver's span covers them.

entries.name: VHF Band III — DAB and television
entries.notes: DAB+ ensembles occupy 1.536 MHz each on the 5A–13F block raster in Region 1; Region 2 uses the band for television channels 7–13.

entries.name: UHF military air band
entries.notes: AM like the civil band, running 225–400 MHz in most administrations. 243.0 MHz is the military emergency frequency.

entries.name: ILS glide path
entries.notes: Paired with a localizer in 108–112 MHz; the pairing is fixed by ICAO.

entries.name: Meteorological aids — radiosondes
entries.notes: Vaisala RS41 and Graw DFM sondes transmit GFSK here twice a day from every upper-air station in the world.

entries.name: Emergency beacons — 406 MHz
entries.notes: COSPAS-SARSAT distress beacons. Listening is legal everywhere; transmitting anything here is not.

entries.name: 70 cm amateur
entries.notes: Allocated to the amateur service in all three regions; Regions 2 and 3 extend it to 420–450 MHz. Shared with ISM devices in Region 1.

entries.name: UHF television
entries.notes: 8 MHz channels in Regions 1 and 3, 6 MHz in Region 2.

entries.name: Land mobile and short-range devices (860–890 MHz)
900 MHz cellular
entries.notes: GSM/LTE in Region 1; Region 2 puts the 902–928 MHz ISM band here instead.

entries.name: DME and TACAN
entries.notes: Pulse pairs on a 1 MHz raster, paired with a VOR or ILS.

entries.name: ADS-B and Mode S — 1090 MHz
entries.notes: Transponder replies and extended squitter, 1 Mbit/s PPM. Needs the receiver's own samples at 2 Msps or more, so the channel takes IQ rather than a narrow passband.

entries.name: GNSS — L5, E5 and L2
entries.notes: GPS L5 at 1176.45 MHz, Galileo E5, GLONASS L2 around 1246 MHz.

entries.name: 23 cm amateur
entries.notes: Secondary to radionavigation, and increasingly squeezed by Galileo. Narrowband work clusters around 1296 MHz.

entries.name: Radio astronomy — hydrogen line
entries.notes: Neutral hydrogen radiates at 1420.406 MHz. A passive band worldwide: no emission is permitted, which is why it is quiet enough to hear the galaxy in.

entries.name: Mobile satellite downlink — Inmarsat
entries.notes: 1544–1545 MHz is reserved for distress and safety traffic.

entries.name: GNSS — L1 and E1
entries.notes: GPS L1 at 1575.42 MHz, GLONASS L1 around 1602 MHz.

entries.name: DECT
entries.notes: Cordless telephony: ten 1.728 MHz carriers, TDMA.

entries.name: S-band space operation and telemetry
entries.notes: 2200–2290 MHz is the space-research downlink most cubesats use.

entries.name: ISM — 2.4 GHz
entries.notes: RR 5.150. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and microwave ovens, and the lower half is also the 13 cm amateur band.

entries.name: Radio astronomy — 2.69 GHz
entries.notes: A passive band: no emission is permitted.

entries.name: S-band radar
entries.notes: Airport surveillance and weather radar.

entries.name: Radio altimeters
entries.notes: Aircraft radio altimeters — the band whose neighbours the 5G C-band rollout argued about.

entries.name: Wi-Fi 5 GHz — upper
entries.notes: Dynamic frequency selection is mandatory: the radar here has priority.

entries.name: ISM — 5.8 GHz
entries.notes: RR 5.150. Also the 6 cm amateur band and where analogue FPV video lives.
